originalGroup.sourceNotice: 2026-10-24新题批次 b002；原创候选，非高考真题；自审及程序检查，不声称独立教师或学生稳定性验证。
originalGroup.material:
A. A place for the cup to come back

When the owner of a small station café introduced reusable cups, she expected the deposit to do most of the work. Customers paid two extra pounds and got the money back when they returned a cup. The cups were strong, easy to wash and popular with regular visitors. Yet after a month, nearly half were still missing.

The owner, Leah, asked customers what had happened. Few had deliberately kept a cup. Some had carried it onto a train and could not return to the same station. Others had left it at an office, then forgotten about it until their next visit. A larger deposit might have encouraged them to remember, but it would also have made a morning drink more expensive.

Leah tried a different approach. Two nearby cafés agreed to accept her cups, and she agreed to accept theirs. A simple sticker showed all three return points. The businesses kept a shared record so that returning a cup at a different café did not leave one owner paying for another owner's customers. No new phone application was required.

Returns increased, although not immediately. For the first week, staff had to explain that any of the three cafés could take a cup back. Leah also placed a return box beside the door, where people could leave a cup without joining the queue for drinks. Customers still had to speak to a staff member if they wanted their deposit in cash.

After three months, the owners chose to continue the arrangement. They had not proved that every customer cared more about waste than before. What they had shown, Leah believed, was narrower and more useful: people were more likely to complete a good intention when the last step fitted into the route they already took.

B. Looking beyond the finished photograph

For a local photography competition, sixteen-year-old Daniel planned to take a picture of the old bus shelter near his home. Its roof had a curved glass panel, and late sunlight made a bright pattern on the pavement. He had seen the pattern many times, but he had never stopped to work out exactly when it appeared.

His first attempt was disappointing. He arrived at five o'clock, the time printed on a photograph he had taken in spring. It was now September, and the light fell on a different part of the shelter. A bus blocked the view just as he pressed the button. Daniel could have removed it later on a computer, but he wanted the photograph to record a real moment.

Over the next week he visited at several different times. He wrote down where the light fell, how long each bus waited and which parts of the shelter remained in shadow. A woman who cleaned the shelter noticed his notebook. She explained that buses stayed longer on Tuesdays because a nearby market brought more passengers. She also pointed out a clear view from a small public path behind the shelter.

Daniel's final photograph included a bus. This time it was not blocking the pattern: its dark side made the bright pavement easier to see. The picture did not win first prize, but the judges praised the way it connected an ordinary structure with the movement of the street.

When his teacher asked what he had learned, Daniel did not describe a new camera setting. He talked about returning to one place, noticing what changed and listening to someone who knew it in a different way. The photograph had taken only a second. Preparing to notice that second, he said, had taken a week.

originalGroup.material:
A. The library that needed a smaller vehicle

The town's mobile library was a large van with shelves along both sides. Every Wednesday it visited three villages, carrying books to people who found the main library difficult to reach. When road repairs closed the entrance to one village, the library team expected to miss only a week. The work, however, was extended twice.

Residents suggested parking at the edge of the village. For some readers that would have been enough, but the walking route included a steep hill. The librarian, Nisha, was especially concerned about readers who used walking aids. Moving the service closer on a map did not necessarily make it easier to use.

A volunteer offered a cargo bicycle with a large covered box. It could use a narrow path that remained open during the repairs. The bicycle could carry far fewer books than the van, so Nisha could not simply move the van's usual selection into the box. She invited readers to request books by telephone a few days before each visit. She also left room for a small changing collection, so that readers could still discover something they had not asked for.

The first delivery revealed another problem. A paper list at the bottom of the box became difficult to find when it rained. The team put books into labelled reusable bags and attached the list inside a waterproof cover. They kept the familiar Wednesday schedule instead of introducing extra visits that volunteers might not be able to maintain.

The bicycle service ended when the road reopened. Its value was not that it could replace every library van. The team kept the request system, which helped them choose books more carefully for all three villages. A temporary restriction had made them ask a lasting question: which part of a service must remain fixed, and which part can change to help the people who use it?

B. What the seedlings could actually tell them

A school gardening club wanted to find out whether used tea leaves helped bean seedlings grow. Its members had seen videos recommending the practice, but they noticed that the videos often compared plants in different pots or different places. They decided to design a comparison of their own.

The club planted twenty beans from the same packet in pots of the same size. Ten pots received a measured amount of dried tea leaves mixed into the soil; the other ten received none. Both sets stood on the same long table. Each day, two students used marked containers to give the pots equal amounts of water. Every few days they exchanged the positions of the pots so that one set would not always receive more light.

Three weeks later, the seedlings with tea leaves were, on average, slightly taller. However, the heights within each set varied greatly, and two seedlings without tea leaves were taller than any of the others. Some members wanted to announce that the tea treatment had worked. Their teacher asked them to look again at the size of the difference and the amount of variation.

Instead of preparing a poster saying 'Tea makes beans grow faster', the students described exactly what they had done and shown. They included the height of every seedling, not just the two most impressive plants. They also noted that they had tested one type of bean in one kind of soil for only three weeks.

Next term, they planned to repeat the comparison and try a second amount of tea leaves. Their first experiment had not given them a simple gardening rule. It had given them something they could use more widely: a way to ask whether a neat conclusion was stronger than the observations supporting it.
